summary: Discovery call focused on KiteWave's need to support large user-facing streaming sessions with periodic bursts. Main concerns: p95 streaming latency (sub-500ms target for short chat fragments), sustained token/sec burst handling, and tradeoffs between Redwood Hosted, Dedicated, and Private for cost and data residency. Team agreed to run comparative benchmarks and exchange security docs.
topics: hosted vs dedicated vs private deployment tradeoffs
transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-05-11 15:00 UTC
Duration: 52 minutes
Attendees: Ava Martinez (Redwood AE), Noah Patel (Redwood SE), Maya Chen (CTO - KiteWave), Ravi Singh (Infra), Ellen Park (ML Eng), Sam Torres (Procurement)

Summary: see metadata summary above.

[00:00] Ava Martinez: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. quick intros, I'm Ava, AE at Redwood, and with me is Noah, our systems SE.
[00:18] Maya Chen: Hi all, Maya here. We're trying to validate whether Redwood Hosted can hit our p95 streaming targets and if not what Dedicated or Private buys us.
[00:28] Noah Patel: Yeah. hi. I'll try to get into the technical bits around batching, KV cache, and how we handle bursts.
[00:36] Ravi Singh: Quick note, we have a pretty bursty pattern, user sessions are mostly streaming voice->text conversions then small generative turn responses, so the tail matters.
[00:47] Ellen Park: Our current target is p95 <= 500ms for the first token and p95 <= 1s for full 128-token responses in streaming mode for our low-latency flows.
[00:58] Ava Martinez: That's helpful, thanks. Is that global or specific region?
[01:03] Maya Chen: Primary NA and EU initially, APAC later. Data residency considerations for EU, and some customers require dedicated tenancy.
[01:12] Sam Torres: We'll also need SOC2 proof and KMS integration — procurement hurdles.
[01:17] Noah Patel: Understood. For Hosted we typically show consistent median low-latency, but for p95 under burst you start to see variance without dedicated pools or smart routing to local regions.
[01:29] Maya Chen: Can you quantify 'variance'? Like what numbers should we expect for a 200-connection burst?
[01:36] Noah Patel: Ballpark — with a medium-sized model (7B-ish), on Redwood Hosted you might see p95 ~ 700-900ms during a sudden 200 concurrent streaming session spike depending on sequence length and token churn. With Dedicated pinned GPUs and our batching/kv cache tuned we often get that down to 300-450ms p95.
[01:53] Ravi Singh: That delta is significant for UX. How much of that is network vs serving runtime?
[01:58] Noah Patel: Roughly split. Network + region routing adds variable ms, especially if cross-region. A lot of the extra stems from queuing on the serving side when bursts exceed concurrent capacity — queue wait contributes to p95. Also model tokenizer and decoding overhead matters with streaming.
[02:16] Ellen Park: And what about token/sec? We have periodic analytic jobs that generate ~10k tokens/sec for short ten-minute bursts.
[02:24] Ava Martinez: So two load profiles: continuous low-latency conversational streaming and episodic high-token bursts. Good to call that out.
[02:30] Maya Chen: Exactly. The burst is what scares procurement — costs and throttling.
[02:36] Sam Torres: Right, we need predictable pricing for that burst window or guarantee capacity.
[02:41] Noah Patel: For that use case Dedicated capacity with reserved nodes + burst credits is common. We can size a pool that absorbs the 10k token/sec for 10 minutes and falls back to hosted. The fallback policy can route to a lower-cost quantized model if capacity's constrained.
[02:57] Maya Chen: Quantized model — do you have guidance on quality regression?
[03:02] Noah Patel: Yes. we have Optimize recommendations; for many workloads 8-bit quant gives negligible perf hit but 4-bit may have visible regression on some tasks. We'll run a quick eval on your prompt set.
[03:13] Ravi Singh: Network topology: if we go Private (VPC), what changes? e.g., egress, KMS, audit logs?
[03:21] Noah Patel: Private deployment gives you a customer-controlled VPC and optional on-prem package. KMS/HSM integration for key custody and full audit logs. Latency will depend on where you colocate — on-premizes close to users will lower network latency, but ops overhead increases.
[03:39] Maya Chen: Ops overhead is not trivial now, but security requirements might force Private for some customers.
[03:44] Ava Martinez: On the compliance docs, we'll send SOC2 and ISO artifacts and an architecture checklist for Private deployments after the call.
[03:52] Sam Torres: Appreciate that. Procurement will need the data residency statement for EU customers.
[03:57] Noah Patel: Noted. Back to benchmarks: we propose two quick runs — 1) streaming p95 with 200-400 concurrent WebSocket sessions, measuring first-token and full-response p95s; 2) burst token throughput: 10k tokens/sec sustained for 10 minutes, measuring degradation and tail.
[04:17] Maya Chen: Sounds good. Can Redwood provide the harness or do we need to build our own?
[04:22] Ava Martinez: We can provide a test harness, sample prompts, and a dedicated test project on Hosted. For Dedicated we can spin a small cluster under a pilot agreement.
[04:32] Ravi Singh: For the harness, we need to emulate real user traffic (lots of small responses, some 128-token replies). Also honor our auth and VPC NAT patterns — do you support client IP preservation for affinity?
[04:45] Noah Patel: We have routing knobs for session affinity and sticky routing to reduce cold KV misses. Client IP preservation depends on the deployment; in Private you control the network for sure.
[04:56] Ellen Park: A practical question — what p95 should we realistically promise our product team if we use Redwood Hosted?
[05:03] Noah Patel: If you stay in a single region and keep concurrency per model below the instance's sweet spot, we commonly see p95 ~450–700ms for streaming first-token on 7B models. For tight p95 < 400ms you'd want Dedicated or a smaller model variant for short prompts.
[05:20] Maya Chen: What about model switching? Automatic fallback to cheaper variants isn't going to ruin output quality?
[05:26] Noah Patel: We recommend canary tests; Redwood can fall back to a quantized variant with similar architecture. For many prompts it's fine, but for domain-specific legal text you'd want the high-fidelity model pinned.
[05:37] Sam Torres: Regarding SLAs — if we commit to Dedicated, what's typical uptime and p95 guarantees?
[05:44] Ava Martinez: Dedicated comes with SLA-backed uptime and latency targets in the enterprise contract. We'll draft specifics in the pilot proposal.
[05:50] Maya Chen: Network egress costs — who bears that in Hosted vs Private?
[05:55] Ava Martinez: In Hosted, egress to your customers is usually passed through at cost; for Dedicated we can include negotiation in contract; Private you'd manage egress entirely. We can show a cost model based on your traffic numbers.
[06:08] Ravi Singh: Let's talk concurrency sizing. For 300 concurrent streaming sessions with 1-2 token/sec each, but spikes to 500 concurrent during peaks, how many GPUs?
[06:18] Noah Patel: Depends on model size and quantization. For a 7B on A100-class equiv, continuous 300 streams might need 2-3 GPUs with continuous batching; spikes to 500 would need headroom — so a 4 GPU pool or autoscale policy with burst credits. We'll produce a sizing calc.
[06:33] Ellen Park: Do you support continuous batching for small tokens or will batching introduce extra latency?
[06:39] Noah Patel: Continuous batching reduces cost without adding perceptible latency if tuned correctly. For streaming, we keep micro-batch windows small; your p95 requirements drive the batch window.
[06:48] Maya Chen: Any limitations on WebSocket vs HTTP streaming?
[06:52] Noah Patel: WebSocket is preferred for low-latency persistent sessions. HTTP chunked streaming also supported but you'll see slightly higher connection setup overhead.
[06:59] Ravi Singh: We also want to instrument token-level tracing and per-token cost breakdowns. Is that in Console?
[07:06] Ava Martinez: Yes, Redwood Console exposes token-level cost/latency breakdown, per-route and per-model dashboards. We can provision access for your SREs.
[07:13] Ellen Park: Nice. Is there an SDK for reconciling stream reconnection, resume tokens?
[07:17] Noah Patel: We have client helpers and docs around reconnection and resume tokens, though some integrations are bespoke. We'll share code snippets.
[07:24] Maya Chen: Let's dig into benchmarks — what metrics exactly will you capture in the tests?
[07:29] Noah Patel: p50/p95/p99 for first token and full response, tokens/sec, GPU utilization, queue wait times, KV cache hit ratios, and end-to-end RTT. We'll also capture quality drift when falling back to quantized models.
[07:43] Sam Torres: For procurement, we need an example pricing sheet for Dedicated pilot — rough numbers OK.
[07:48] Ava Martinez: We'll include sample pricing and a pilot agreement template in the follow-up.
[07:53] Maya Chen: Any known gotchas with KMS and private keys for inference encryption?
[07:58] Noah Patel: If you use customer-managed KMS, rotation policies and HSM integrations require setup time. Also some on-prem HSMs may change performance characteristics if every token requires an HSM call — we advise doing envelope encryption so HSM ops are amortized.
[08:16] Ravi Singh: Good point. For our regulatory flows we may need to keep embeddings out of hosted storage — can you restrict retention?
[08:23] Ava Martinez: Yes, retention policies and per-tenant data retention are configurable; Dedicated/Private gives strict isolation.
[08:29] Ellen Park: Could we go into a quick scenario: user session starts, 30s of voice transcription -> short 40-token reply. Walk me through where latency occurs.
[08:37] Noah Patel: Sure. steps: 1) ASR transcribe -> tokens hit your frontend; 2) call Redwood API via websocket -> network latency to region; 3) routing and request scheduling -> possible queue wait if pool saturated; 4) model tokenization and kv cache lookup -> if session warm, KV hits reduce time; 5) decoding/streaming first token back. So key knobs: region proximity, session affinity, KV cache warm starts, and batch window size.
[09:02] Maya Chen: If KV cache is cold, how much penalty?
[09:05] Noah Patel: Can be 30-120ms depending on sequence length and architecture. Cold-starts for very long contexts are heavier.
[09:11] Ravi Singh: We'd like to measure cache warm ratio in the benchmark.
[09:14] Noah Patel: We'll include KV hit metrics.
[09:17] Ava Martinez: Quick check — any blockers from procurement side on shared test accounts?
[09:22] Sam Torres: We need a simple NDA or pilot terms; otherwise legal won't sign off.
[09:27] Ava Martinez: We'll attach a one-page pilot SOW and NDA to the follow-up.
[09:31] Maya Chen: Great. On fallback policies, can we do per-customer routing so premium customers never get quantized fallbacks?
[09:40] Noah Patel: Yes, routing policies can be per-customer with pinning to models or dedicated pools.
[09:44] Ellen Park: For the 10k token/sec burst, what's the typical observable on the tail if you don't have dedicated capacity?
[09:50] Noah Patel: You'll typically see p95 blow out to multiple seconds as queues grow, and some requests may get queued or rate-limited depending on quotas.
[09:58] Maya Chen: That's what we feared. So Dedicated seems likely, but procurement needs numbers.
[10:03] Ava Martinez: We'll provide cost estimates for a pilot Dedicated pool sized for your burst.
[10:08] Ravi Singh: Are there any integrations for sidecar caching or client-side batching?
[10:12] Noah Patel: Yes, we support prefix caching and recommend client-side micro-batching where applicable. We'll share best-practice docs.
[10:19] Maya Chen: Any surprises around model serialization or quantized kernel compatibility?
[10:24] Noah Patel: Some older kernels mis-handle attention patterns; Redwood's runtime picks optimized kernels based on architecture and sequence distribution, but we'll validate your model variants during onboarding.
[10:36] Ellen Park: Could we get a rough timeline for pilot to production?
[10:40] Ava Martinez: Typical pilot (benchmarks + small Dedicated pilot) is 3-6 weeks, then production depends on contract and infra work — maybe additional 2-6 weeks.
[10:51] Sam Torres: Noted. Procurement will want a single point of contact to expedite the SOW.
[10:56] Ava Martinez: That'll be me.
[10:58] Maya Chen: Thanks. Any quick wins we can take now?
[11:01] Noah Patel: We can start with a Hosted benchmark to get concrete numbers, then propose Dedicated sizing. Also small prompt rewrites to reduce token length can cut costs immediately.
[11:10] Ellen Park: We'll extract a prompt sample and usage histograms and share them after this call.
[11:15] Maya Chen: Good.
[11:17] Ava Martinez: I'll summarize action items and next steps in an email.
[11:21] Sam Torres: Thanks everyone.
[11:25] Maya Chen: Quick minor note — sometimes the call transcription renames Redwood product names, we saw 'Redwood Dedi' in a previous note, just an FYI.
[11:33] Noah Patel: (laughs) we get that.
[11:36] Ava Martinez: Alright, we'll follow up with the harness and docs.
[11:40] Maya Chen: Thanks all.

End of transcript.
